text: A rabbi hears Hitler Youth chanting outside his own house during Purim and concludes, without much strain, that Germany will hold. Peter Lilienthal grants him that conviction for a long while, then takes it apart at the speed of administration rather than of violence: a school roll his son is struck from, an order, an address that has become a fact on someone's list. The Golden Bear went to this. What the film does with 127 minutes is refuse the compression that would make the story bearable, so that fear registers as weather rather than as incident, something carried through ordinary afternoons and errands. And it stays with David, left to work out what leaving costs and who can still be asked for anything, in a country that in most rooms still looks like home.

The banquet is for an association of anglers, which is to say for men who have formally organized themselves around waiting. José Luis García Sánchez keeps the film inside the restaurant that has to produce it, and farce of this kind runs on a single engine: an occasion that must go correctly, and a building full of people with reasons why it will not. Kitchens are useful rooms for that. They are hierarchical, they run on timing, and they put the served and the serving on either side of one door. The Golden Bear went to Las truchas, a Spanish comedy of 1978 that spends ninety-nine minutes on an official dinner coming slowly apart while everyone at the table maintains the position that it is going well.

One soldier walks out of captivity carrying another soldier's name, then walks with it into that man's house. The deception in Rainer Simon's film is not a trick but an intimacy: Karl arrives knowing what a husband would know, and Anna, who has spent the war refusing to believe she is a widow, has reasons of her own to let the details settle. Die Frau und der Fremde shared the top prize at Berlin in 1985. Ninety-seven minutes, largely two people in rooms, and the weight rests on what she will accept and what he will keep saying out loud. It is built so that cruelty and mercy become the same act performed by the same man, which is hard to hold in balance and is why the film stays quiet where a thriller would get loud.

A woman who has never had to ask how she came to own part of Ireland begins, during the First World War, to find out. Her class called itself the Ascendancy, British landowners on Irish ground, and Edward Bennett places his protagonist inside that arrangement rather than across from it. The Golden Bear went to the film in 1983. Ninety-two minutes is brief for a political education, which suggests rooms, silences and withheld information rather than events; the independence movement she comes to learn about was not new, and her not having noticed it was something her position had arranged on her behalf. What she stands to lose by learning is not her life. It is everything else she has been given.

The bomb goes off early, and most of what follows is procedure: statements, hearings, the machinery that turns a death into a case. Fatih Akin gives Katja a husband and a son and takes them away in the first movement, which leaves 106 minutes for the harder problem, which is what a person does with the interval between a loss and any answer to it while the answer is being administered by other people at their own speed. Audiences across Europe voted it the People's Choice at the European Film Awards and Germany sent it to the Academy Awards; the record singles out the lead performance, which is the right place to look, since a film built this way lives on one face holding the frame while institutions work around it. Revenge, in a structure like this, is less a plan than a symptom.

Getting two parents out of a police station turns out to have a price, an actual figure, and much of this film is four young people moving around Manila to assemble it. The store Rosa keeps is small and everyone in the neighborhood knows her, and the narcotics she and Nestor resell on the side are small too, which is the point: the arrest is not the discovery of a cartel but the activation of a business that runs in the other direction, outward from the station. Brillante Ma Mendoza spends 110 minutes on the shoe leather of that, and the Philippines sent the result to the Academy Awards. What the record marks is the performance at the center, a woman required to keep being a mother in a room where she is being priced.

Every apartment in the building has been sold to the developers except one, and the woman who owns that one is not moving. That is the entire engine, and Kleber Mendonça Filho is content to run it for 147 minutes, long enough for the developers' patience to become a kind of weather and long enough for Clara to exceed her position in the plot. She was a music critic, which is a working life spent attending to what other people treat as background. She is also a widow, and in a story about property that is never only a private fact. It took the Grande Prêmio do Cinema Brasileiro for Best Film. The pressure here is not really eviction; it is the slower question of whether a person is permitted to stay where her life has already happened.

Debt collection is entry-level work for the Triads, and it is what Autumn Moon does after he stops going to school. Fruit Chan keeps the whole film at that height: housing estates, stairwells, errands, small sums owed by people who plainly cannot pay them, a teenager with no plan past the next round. Three separate bodies in Hong Kong named it the best film of its year, and the Golden Horse list of a hundred great Chinese-language films holds it. The year is 1997, which in this city needs no annotation. The charge in the film comes less from crime than from arithmetic, the way a debt, an illness and a favor owed to older men all convert into one currency, and the way that currency is always somebody's body.

Chinatown in New York is neither America nor Hong Kong, and a student who arrives from one to attend college in the other has to live in the gap. Mabel Cheung Yuen-Ting builds on that displacement rather than on incident: Lee Kay has classes, a boyfriend who turns out to be unfaithful, and a cousin already living nearby who is around when it happens. Ninety-eight minutes, mostly streets and rented rooms and the long middle distance between two people from one city who have ended up in very different lives in another. It took best picture at the Hong Kong Film Awards and sits on the Golden Horse hundred. The risk in a premise like this is sentiment. The material underneath it is closer to class, and to what each of them can afford to want.

A photographer returns to a country he has already photographed once, at a moment when the story is supposed to be finished. Ann Hui makes the visitor's job into the film's method: he has come to document a nation after its liberation, and the version he is offered keeps failing to contain one poor family whose children he begins following instead. That is an unusually honest structure, since it puts a foreign professional with a camera and an exit among people who have neither. 109 minutes, made in Hong Kong in 1982, best picture at the Hong Kong Film Awards, and a place on the Golden Horse hundred. What is at stake is not his safety. It is whether pictures taken by someone who can leave are worth anything to the people who cannot.

1943, a village in Bulgaria, and a German sergeant with a sketchbook is having an almost comfortable war. Then a transit camp is set up nearby for Jews arriving from Greece, and Konrad Wolf places his film precisely on the seam between a man's private decency and what he is billeted to. The request that reaches Walter is a small one, help for a pregnant woman, and Ruth is the one who makes it; the ninety-two minutes hold to the position that small requests are where a person is actually decided. It carries a jury prize and a place on the German canon list Die wichtigsten deutschen Filme. The premise allows him almost no heroism: he can be kind at nearly no cost, up to the moment kindness costs something.

It is filed as a comedy and it earns the label, in the sense that the talk is genuinely funny and nothing the talk does to people is. Mike Leigh gives his man 131 minutes and one night of London to cross, no work, no destination, and a mind quick enough to take apart anyone who stops to listen. The film sits on TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest Films and the record marks the lead performance, which is where the trouble is: cruelty delivered at that speed is a pleasure to watch, and the film knows it and declines to protect anyone in the audience from knowing it. No arc here bends toward repair. What it moves toward is morning, and the accumulated cost of a night spent being cleverer than everyone in the room.
